# **Precious metal report** _Gold, silver, platinum and palladium November 2011_ **David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** **09 December 2011** #### **New York:** • In price terms, gold outperformed the other precious metals during November. Despite rapidly rising levels of concern over the Euro debt crisis, an almost continual increase in the Dollar’s value against the Euro offset risk-driven buying for gold, with the price of the yellow metal trading neutrally across the month, albeit in a wide range. The other three metals all lost ground as their greater exposure to industrial demand and their lower safe haven status made them more vulnerable to negative sentiment. • The December 8th and 9th European summits failed to come to an agreement amongst all the European Union’s member states over the way forward. An agreement between the Euro member states and some non-Euro members of the Union has started to lay the early groundwork for a solution to the Eurozone’s problems. However, expect the market to be disappointed with progress in the short term and for gold to outperform the rest of the precious metal complex. • Supply side nationalism is becoming an increasing issue in the mining sector. Protests at a Peruvian gold project, the imposition of higher taxes and royalties in a range of countries and nationalisation/ indigenisation debates in others are making operating a mine an ever more uncertain economic activity. **_Figure 2_** _: Dollar strength against the Euro should not surprise anyone._ Some of the effects of the continuing crisis are entirely predictable. November saw good buying of gold to ameliorate risk and also saw the Dollar strengthening against the Euro as investors reacted entirely logically. With this safe haven buying to support it, the gold price (in Dollar terms) was buffeted by market events but did not lose ground. The other metals, more reliant on industrial demand and with less of a safe haven bid lost ground. The outlook for the remainder of the year is somewhat uncertain as liquidity issues have also driven some investors to reduce positions. However, gold seems set to outperform the rest of the precious metals complex almost no matter what the outcome from the various European summit meetings are. Governments and Central Banks legislated to force the banking system to rebuild its reserve ratios, a laudable longer term objective to reinforce financial stability. However, at the same time, they tried to inject liquidity into the market. Many banks reacted entirely logically in trying to rebuild their capital levels ahead of new rules to take effect next year by cutting back on their lending to customers. They also slowed their lending to one another to avoid credit risk with any banks which could be over-exposed to European sovereign debt or short-term funding, another rational response. The response of policy makers and the markets is, though, not fully rational but bounded by politically-acceptable choices, the legal structures of the bodies involved and the time available. Viewed in this light, the limits of the German constitutional courts on bail-outs, the ECB’s limitations on its bond buying programme and the UK’s intransigence on treaty changes should not be ignored as huge obstacles to a quick resolution of the European problems. The European summit which is taking place on the 8th and 9th of December has been promoted like a summer blockbuster film, along the lines of “xxx days to save the Euro”. A reasonable question for the markets to ask is why, after a string of earlier summits, this should be any different in terms of producing and starting to implement a viable solution to the current Euro problems. Although a greater sense of political determination to is evident, it is not clear how many

of the proposed suggestions could be implemented within the constraints of the single market on a timescale acceptable to the financial markets. In particular, the likelihood of full scale QEE (QE Europaeisch), a European bout of quantitative easing seems further away than many hopeful and hungry investors would like to think, even though the ECB and other central banks are helping improve liquidity in the banking sector already. 



3 

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** 

**09 December 2011** 

Having spent part of my working life commuting to Brussels and sometimes dealing with the European Union, I firmly believe that the continued existence of a viable Europe is an almost religious belief of many European politicians. As a result, in times of crisis, they may be able to convince themselves of the necessity to circumnavigate normal rules of democratic governance or procedure in order to protect this ideal. We believe that these politicians will, eventually, come to an agreement that allows the Euro to continue as a single currency with all of its current members. How this is achieved is not yet clear but we expect to see greater fiscal integration and the tighter enforcement of rules on budget deficits and accounting as has been proposed. 

It is likely that the increased pressure from the bond markets and on the banking sector will generate an additional sense of urgency amongst Europe’s political leaders this week. We should therefore see some progress being made towards a viable longer term solution. However, addressing the shorter term issues of liquidity and solvency are rather more urgent and here progress is expected to be slimmer. 

The slightly discordant noises coming from the Franco-German mini-summit at the start of December illustrate the challenges in reaching agreement between even two member states, let alone seventeen Euro members or all twenty-seven (or twenty-eight now that Croatia has joined) European Union countries: already Ireland has mentioned the possibility of a national referendum on any agreement. The key question, though will be whether enough progress can be made on a future structure for the Eurozone to convince German legislators to loosen the purse-strings or to encourage or allow the ECB to act as a lender of last resort to the countries of the Eurozone. 

We expect the market to be disappointed. Hopes of a resolution are overblown, although progress has been made. We expect that a resolution to the liquidity problems and the threat of sovereign default of a larger nation will eventually be found. We feel, though that this is a longer term project than many expect and that we could in the short term see a weaker Euro and more risk-based buying. Expect gold to outperform in this situation.

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report**

## **<mark>Gold</mark>** 

In overall price terms, gold had a fairly neutral month during Nove

mber. It started at $1,720 and traded as high as $1,800 and as low as $1,670 before closing the month with an upwards rush from $1,706 to $1,748 on the last day of the month to give a marginally bullish tone. In Euro terms, gold performed much more strongly, rising from €1,235 to a touch over €1,300, demonstrating the global appetite for gold from investors and speculators. Surprisingly, perhaps, gold has not, however, recaptured its highs of September even in Euro terms despite a succession of European governments falling like dominoes. Gold Price(USD/oz)

**_Figure 3_** _: The gold price in Dollar terms has underperformed expectations despite buying interest as the Euro has weakened._ **_Figure 4_** _: In Euro terms, gold has performed more strongly as nervous Europeans try to hedge their Euro exposure_ The Euro debt crisis was the key issue throughout the month, with two rapid $100 moves buffeting the market. At the end of October, the market had relaxed a little when agreement was reached over a Greek bailout. Almost immediately the Greek Prime Minister decided to put this to a popular vote, sending other European politicians into a mixture of fury and panic and driving gold higher. On the 3rd , the European Central Bank (ECB) cut interest rates. Counter-intuitively, the Euro rose on the signs that at least someone understood the gravity of the situation. Gold shot to $1,760 that day and the upwards move eventually came to a stop at $1,800 on the 8th . On the 9th , though, Italy’s emergency budget failed to convince the markets. Bond yields soared and the Euro lurched lower, sending gold back to $1,745 the following day before yet another European leader – Berlusconi on this occasion – revealed that he would resign. The Euro showed some brief unexpected strength and gold recovered a little. How- 5 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **09 December 2011** ever, the Dollar soon started to strengthen once again and gold weakened. Speculation that the EFSF might not rescue Italy, and that US banks might yet catch a cold if Europe sneezes, drove selling across many asset markets. Gold was no exception and it fell to $1,672 on the 21st as investors looked to cover losses in other markets. While the gold price has been volatile, it has typically recovered well from these multiasset sell-offs this year, and November was no exception. Investor concern over slowing growth, sovereign debt, and any number of other issues, combined to drive more gold b

uying. Gold slowly ground its way back to $1,720 on the 30<sup>th</sup> . The last action of the month was more explosive, though: a group of the largest central banks made an announcement of a concerted decision to inject much more liquidity into the world’s financial system. With the immediate threat of bank insolvency reduced or removed, every asset market reacted positively with gold shooting higher to end the month just above $1,745. 

Looking forward, though, the question must be whether continued Euro stress (or less likely, the resolution of this issue) should be positive or negative for gold. If the debt problems continue, then the appetite for gold as an asset should rise but the Euro should weaken. If a resolution can be seen, or even early signs of a resolution appear, then gold could lose some supporters but the Euro should strengthen. In both cases, currency movements should offset some of the buying or selling interest in gold. On balance, however, we remain bullish for gold in the near term once the most immediate risk event (the 9<sup>th</sup> December summit) has passed. There are plenty of reasons to buy and hold gold in the current environment and these should start to reassert themselves once the short term uncertainty starts to diminish. 

### **Asian gold demand** 

High gold prices and persistent inflation are having a varied set of impacts across Asia’s gold markets. In Vietnam, a lack of confidence in the local currency has driven speculation in gold and the Government is continuing its efforts to increase its control of this trade. The most recent action is the selection of SJC, a local refiner to produce gold bars under the guidance of the State Bank. Although this refinery already has a dominant position in the local market, an exclusive licence should allow the state to  control the domestic gold market more effectively. In the Philippines, Central Bank buying of gold from local producers was 1.7 tonnes in Q3 2011 compared to 7.2 tonnes a year earlier, which the Government suggests is due to smuggling of metal out of the country due to high prices. 

In South Korea, a more developed economy, gold plays less of a financial role and consumers seem to be reacting to high metal prices by reining in their purchases of jewellery. There are indications of lower carating, where consumers are buying lower purity gold jewellery than they might normally purchase, in an effort to keep costs down. Apparently it is traditional to give children a one don (3.75g) gold ring on their first birthday but jewellers are now manufacturing 1g rings for more cost-conscious purchasers. Overall, these trends fit with the World Gold Council’s view that Q3 demand for gold jewellery in South Korea fell from 3.4 tonnes in 2010 to 2.8 tonnes this year. 

In Japan, although jewellery sales remain fairly healthy, consumers are selling back large amounts of jewellery which was bought during the bubble economy more than twenty years ago. According to G

overnment statistics, more than 95 tonnes of gold have been exported from Japan in the first ten months of the year, their highest ever level. With gold prices still below their 1980 highs, we feel that further price increases will encourage further sales of old jewellery and bullion as some consumers and investors take the opportunity to make a nominal “profit” after thirty years. Indications from India suggest that price sensitivity has started to appear in this key market for gold. As we reported in our October monthly report, sales of gold during Diwali were lower in weight terms than they were one year earlier. To show the rapid pace of change and huge price sensitivity of this market, only a month ago, the Bombay Bullion 6 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **09 December 2011** Association was forecasting that imports of gold into India could reach one thousand tonnes. The latest forecast is that they could instead fall by ten per cent from last year’s levels to 850-900 tonnes, with imports in the third quarter having fallen to 200 tonnes. A large part of the price appreciation has been driven by the Rupee’s rapid slide against the US Dollar in recent weeks which has made gold more expensive in local currency terms and has driven larger flows of scrap material. 7 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **09 December 2011** ### **Official sector buying** Recent news confirms that the official sector continues to be a buyer of gold. The Bank of Korea (South Korea) revealed that it bought 15 tonnes of gold in November, its second purchase this year and also only its second in more than ten years. D

uring 2011, it has bought 40 tonnes of gold, taking its reserves up to 54 tonnes. Other countries have been buying too, particularly those which are running a budget surplus and have to expand their reserves yet do not wish to become over-exposed to the US Dollar or the shakier Euro. In October, the list of these net buyers included, at a minimum, Belarus, Colombia, Kazakhstan, Mexico, Russia, Tajikistan, Ukraine and Malta. 

### **Supply side nationalism** 

Recent press stories about the triumphal return of some of Venezuela’s gold reserves to “popular acclaim” and signs saying “The gold has returned thanks to Chavez” illustrates the important role that gold often plays in a nation’s psychology. As we commented earlier this year, resource nationalism is a rising force with an increasing number of countries looking to capture the economic benefits of mineral resources found on their territory. Gold is at particular risk because of its status as a pseudo-currency and this could start to pose increasing problems for the development of new mines in many jurisdictions around the world. Recently, Newmont’s proposed Conga mine in Peru has been in the news with locals objecting to its development on environmental grounds. The project was suspended at the start of December after rioting nearby. 

Elsewhere in South America, Kinross seems likely to sign a deal with the Ecuadorean Government to develop the Fruta del Norte gold mine. Production should start in 2014. While this does indicate that new mines can be developed, comments that the Government will receive a minimum of 52 per cent of the economic benefits of the project through taxation, royalties and other payments are worrying. The deal is apparently set to include a windfall tax where 70 per cent of the profits above $1,650 (or the spot price when the contract is signed) go to the Government. 

In Africa, Ghana introduced its own windfall tax of ten per cent and increased the corporate tax rate for miners by a further ten per cent. Taxation on capital investment will change too. Exact details of the new tax regime are hard to find but Goldfields has already commented that some of its investment plans within Ghana could be adversely affected by the proposals. 

Overall, we see this trend of resource nationalism intensifying (as can be seen in the nationalisation debate in South Africa or the indigenisation process in Zimbabwe). Gold is an emotive material and high prices are likely to make raising the tax take from mining this mineral increasingly tempting to governments everywhere. This would add to production costs and decrease growth in mine production within the industry, helping to support gold at higher prices than would otherwise be the case. 

### **Gold investment** 

ETF investment in gold seems to play a hybrid or intermediate role between real physical investment and the futures market. Given the risk evident in the wider marketplace – as shown by rising European bond yields and gener

al high levels of financial asset price volatility – it was unsurprising to see ETF buying throughout most of October and the whole of November. During that period, there was net buying for eight consecutive weeks, during which period global holdings climbed from 67.1 million ounces to 70.3 million ounces. From then on, the price action was mainly downwards. Having outperformed gold

in a rising market in October, silver instead underperformed gold in a falling market in November. The silver:gold ratio moved fairly steadily in gold’s favour from an initial 50:1 to a closing 53:1. An increasingly gloomy economic outlook and a softening of industrial demand for silver were accompanied by a slowing of physical investment demand, making silver less able to fight the effects of a strengthening US Dollar. **_Figure 11_** _: Silver has failed to recover most of the ground it lost in price terms during September._ By its own remarkable recent standards, price movements were relatively limited. Early the month, silver briefly touched a low of $32.30 on the 1st after the incredulous market reaction to the Greek Prime Minister’s attempt to resuscitate Greek democracy with a referendum on the proposed bail-out before recovering to $34.30 the following day. As successive European governments fell, silver traded in a $1.50 range around $34.50 until the 17th. At that point, the market panicked when rumours swirled that the EFSF would not choose to bail out the Italian Government. Bond yields soared and many different assets were sold off. Silver did not escape and collapsed to $31.50 later that day. It proved unable to gain any traction for the remainder of the month and traded it out in a $2 range either side of $32 per ounce. **_Figure 13_** _: All of the other precious metals have suffered in comparison to gold as investors have become increasingly concerned about the wider effects of European sovereign debt problems._ As European bank recapitalisation has proceeded, and the existential risks to the continent’s banking system have increased, the prospects for global growth have worsened significantly. At the same time, risk has increased dramatically, culminating in a desire to hold safe haven assets as ever more apocalyptic comments are made about the Euro. In this environment of heightened risk and softening industrial demand it is not surprising that silver has recently underperformed gold in price terms. Looking into next year, we are bullish for gold and therefore, to a degree at least, bullish for silver. To determine how bullish we are for the white metal, we need to understand how gold and silver prices are likely to be correlated. In our view, the market has overestimated the likelihood of a Euro break-up and it is therefore overestimating the amount of risk present in the current political environment and it is simultaneously underestimating the rate of economic growth that will take place. In the short term, underlying reality is unimportant, however: if the market believes something then it will price this in. We would expect silver to continue to underperform in the short term while this mindset continues. As the threat of a Euro break-up recedes, the reality of underlying economic growth should be more noticeable and we would expect silver to start to outperform gold later in 2012. ### **GFMS silver forecast** GFMS recently unveiled its latest forecast for the silver market. ### **The purpose of silver miners** 

All too often in the mining industry, primary producers focus on digging ounces of metal out of the ground (and refining it) as their mission. The alternative, and more commercial view, is that the purpose of almost any company is to make a sustainable profit and to increase its owners’ or shareholders’ capital. 

Viewed in this light, the recent proposal by Eric Sprott of Sprott Asset Management makes interesting reading. He suggests that silver producers, many of whom are currently generating large amounts of free cash flow, would be better served by holding their reserves (or a portion of them) in silver instead of in cash. This could serve several purposes: it removes some of the solvency risk of holding cash for anyone concerned about the immediate health of the financial sector; if governments are to try to inflate away some of their debts, then hard, “cash-like” assets such as silver could gain in value compared to their cash equivalent; and the removal of some metal from the market could, as with ETFs, improve the market balance for silver, helping it to appreciate further in price terms. In effect, this action would be a hedge, not dissimilar to a producer buying forward metal by using their cash flows. 

When questioned about this proposal at a recent results presentation, one major producer suggested that it could consider such a move under certain conditions or, at least, it would not rule it out. While we agree with the thesis that the precious metals could continue to gain in nominal terms and that there could be some economic benefits, we find this proposal odd both from a theoretical point of view and a practical point of view. 

From a theoretical point of view, it is hard to see why mining a material and simply storing it above ground should be an economically-meaningful activity. While it could add financial value under some circumstances and there could be an economic argument for this approach, it is hard to find a moral argument for the expenditure of effort required to mine, refine and then simply store the material produced. 

From a practical point of view it seems an unlikely approach too. The move from producer hedging to a neutral position has been driven both by the industry’s poor experience of hedging on occasions in the past and by investors’ attitudes. Larger holders of mining

they are equally capable of carrying this out themselves. ### **Silver investment** For anyone looking for silver to exhibit pure “safe haven” characteristics, a comparison of ETF flows for silver and gold in the last few weeks would be instructive. While gold recorded eight consecutive weeks of net inflows into global funds, silver saw net selling for six of those eight weeks. For November as a whole, silver saw a small net inflow of just under six million ounces, taking total holdings to 460 million ounces, close to the level that they have been since early August. Interestingly, ETF investors do not seem to have been unduly influenced by price movements during that period with the sharp correction in late September having had little impact. As a result, although it is hard to forecast ETF trading volumes in the short term, we feel that an upwards movement in the price would be required to reinvigorate buying interest from silver ETF investors. COMEX open interest remains under half of its September highs and below one third of its February 2011 levels, suggesting that futures investors too require some change in the market before returning in numbers. Short positioning remains limited, though, suggesting that there is little appetite on betting on a falling silver price. Weekly Silver ETF flows (oz)

### **Johnson Matthey’s latest review of the platinum market** 

On November the 15<sup>th</sup> , Johnson Matthey (JM) released its latest review of the platinum market (Platinum 2011 Interim Review). The most recent estimates for the platinum market suggest that gross demand for platinum is expected to grow by 2.2 per cent to 8.08 million ounces, close to pre-crisis levels, in 2011. Open loop recycling should increase by 2.7 per cent to 1.88 million ounces and metal sales from primary mining are set to expand by 5.7 per cent to 6.40 million ounces. Overall, the market is set to move from close to balance last year into a surplus of 195,000 ounces for the year. 

Gross platinum demand from the automotive sector is set to increase this year, rising by 2.8 per cent to 3.16 million ounces. Although the European car market has been weak this year, with widespread economic problems depressing consumers’ willingness to buy new vehicles, the market share of the diesel vehicle increased. Substitution of some of the platinum in a typical diesel catalyst by palladium is continuing and Johnson Matthey expects some 30 per cent of the diesel catalyst market by weight to be palladium this year (with slow progress towards perhaps a fifty per cent share for palladium in a decade’s time). Light duty vehicle platinum demand is expected to be little changed from last year. 

Outside Europe, platinum demand depends on the growth of the diesel car segment, given that gasoline (or three way) catalysts are now almost exclusively palladium/rhodium based. Growth in North American and Indian diesel passenger car sales is therefore positive for platinum demand. Growth in heavy duty diesel vehicle production (up by almost half in North America this year) is now a major component of automotive demand. 

Gross jewellery sector demand for platinum is expected to rise by roughly 1.9 per cent to 2.47 million ounces this year. The North American market has been fairly healthy but European demand has weakened a little. Gross Japanese demand will fall marginally but has been much stronger than might have been expected given the triple disaster that occurred in Q2 2011. More metal will be recycled i

n Japan, though, than in the previous year. 

However, the most important jewellery market remains China. Here, the narrowing (and recent reversal) of platinum’s traditional price differential with gold has been too recent to allow a simple forecast of consumer or manufacturer behaviour. As Zhou Enlai said of the French Revolution’s impact, “It is too early to say”. We note, however, from Mitsui’s own research and Johnson Matthey’s comments, that some of the production capacity that would normally be available for platinum jewellery manufacturing has been diverted to gold production. In our view, this places a limit on the potential output of the platinum jewellery manufacturers in the short term. Overall, Johnson Matthey’s figures indicate that this individual market could grow from a gross 1.65 million ounces to 1.69 million ounces this year. We believe that the market could grow a little faster than this. Recycling rates have fallen so net demand for new metal has risen by roughly ten per cent. 

Industrial demand for platinum should reach a record level following the previous year’s strong growth. It should increase by 11.7 per cent to 1.96 million ounces. Despite gloomladen headlines, the world’s economy has grown this year and there has been a reasonable amount of investment in new capacity for the electronics and chemical industry. In China, a crackdown on credit availability has restricted new building and

### **The European car market** 

There are growing signs of the European car market preparing itself for a sharp downturn. While many of the automotive manufacturers have seen strong production and healthy profits this year, supported by exports to China, there have recently been a few announcements of cuts being made to forthcoming production. Currently, these are only small adjustments but with a European recession increasingly likely, the mood is becoming noticeably bleaker. 

In this environment, J.D.Power recently revised its 2012 European sales forecast downwards from a 2 per cent fall to a 5 per cent decrease in sales to 12.15 million units. They acknowledge the possibility of a sharper fall in new vehicle sales if the recession is deeper than expected. Interestingly/depressingly, this lower forecast would see sales only at the level of mid-2008, the point at which many European national governments acted to introduce scrappage/subsidy schemes. The main positives for the industry are that the Chinese automotive market looks set to resume decent rates of growth next year and that the majority of European car makers are in a better financial position than they were before the global economic crisis. 

Data from the European car market shows the negative impact of the ongoing debt crisis on consumer confidence within Europe, though: 10.1 million passenger cars were sold in the region during the first nine months of the year, a decline of a little over one per cent compared to the same period one year earlier. Sales are now falling more quickly. 

Within Europe, fleet car sales have become more important in supporting new car demand and, in particular demand for diesel vehicles. According to AID (www.eagleaid.com), an automotive industry newsletter, the European market share of diesel passenger cars climbed to a record 55.2 per cent in the first nine months of this year, roughly four per cent more than was the case last year, helping to support platinum demand in this region. 

In its most recent report on the platinum group metals market, Johnson Matthey estimated that demand for platinum from the European heavy duty diesel manufacturers climbed by 40 per cent to almost 50,000 ounces. The most recent data on this market indicates that it is still recovering well with sales of commercial vehicles within Europe 7.5 per cent above 2010 levels for the year-to-date. While this market accounts for a relatively small proportion of the total of nearly 1.5 million ounces of platinum used by the European automotive industry in a typical year, growth in the commercial vehicle sector will continue to support platinum demand. 

Overall, we are somewhat bearish for platinum demand from this sector for the first half of next year at least while we are more neutral on palladium demand.

### **The global automotive market** 

In all the gloom of a European debt crisis, it is easy to imagine that the world car industry is underperforming this year. However, this is a long way from the truth, with many markets performing well. In recent months, though, there has been an abrupt change with some of the faster growing markets, Brazil, China and India slowing or even moving into reverse. In China, efforts to tame high inflation have resulted in lower credit availability and a slowdown in car sales. Within Brazil, an overheating economy seems to have had the same effect and what look suspiciously like protectionist policies will hurt the market further. Indian car sales are now starting to fall year-on-year with high fuel prices and high interest rates largely to blame. The Thai floods have also hurt South-East Asian light duty vehicle output  although this should be only a short term issue. 

Other markets are rather healthier though. Russian car sales continue to grow strongly and Russia is on course, eventually, to be the largest national market within Europe. The Japanese market is on course for recovery, albeit with further disruptions from the Thai floods. The USA and the rest of North America are also performing surprisingly well. November sales in the USA were 995,000 units, 14 per cent more than were sold a year earlier. Growth rates are also higher for trucks than for passenger cars, meaning that average palladium loadings are rising. There are, though, some dark clouds on the horizon: this good pace of growth is from a very low base and the market remains smaller than its pre-crisis size. Inventory of unsold cars climbed to 57 days worth of stock from 50 in October. Thanksgiving does disrupt the November statistics but further increases in these inventory levels would cause us to downgrade our forecasts for palladium use in this market next year. We are currently bullish for palladium demand from this sector for 2012.

### **Palladium jewellery in China** 

The long, steady decline in manufacturing and retail volumes of palladium jewellery within China continued in the four months from July to October 2011. Manufacturing volumes were roughly 15-20 per cent lower than a year earlier although they were some 10 per cent stronger than in the previous four month period. Relatively few companies are now producing palladium jewellery with some now only producing pieces to order. With only this small number of manufacturers still active in this market, there has been little pressure on margins which are essentially unchanged in recent months. Despite falling demand, there therefore seems little prospect of further companies exiting the palladium jewellery market in the short term. 

The outlook for the next few months is more positive as the lower palladium price has made jewellery made from this metal more cost-competitive. More importantly, the forthcoming Chinese New Year and Valentine’s Day sales seasons should encourage more buying by retailers and wholesalers to build stocks. 

There has been little if any change to manufacturers’ stocks of palladium, whether inprocess materials or finished goods. The decrease in the size of this market means that an increasing proportion of business is manufacturing to order (instead of manufacturing for stocks which are sold to retailer purchasing managers visiting Shenzhen). There is little scope now for further reductions in stocks of finished palladium pieces but, as demand dwindles, we would expect to see a slow decrease in working stocks of metal. 

A major change is an increase of between ten and twenty per cent in the amount of recycled palladium being used by the industry from July to October compared to the previous four month period (the latest Johnson Matthey figures suggest over a hundred per cent increase in the use of recycled palladium this year). High metal prices (compared to last year) have driven retailers and wholesalers to recycle and remanufacture old stock and an increasing propor

tion of manufacturing is from cannibalisation of this old, unsold stock. The recent price fall may decrease the industry’s desire to recycle this material. In any case, as this market shrinks in size, the amount of metal available for recycling will shrink. 

We do not expect the recent fall in the price of palladium to reignite consumer demand for palladium jewellery.
